content: Endometritis refers to the inflammation of the uterine lining, which can extend to all layers of the uterus. Normally, the uterus is aseptic, but microbial migration from the cervix and vagina can result in infection and inflammation. Histopathologically, endometritis is categorized into two subtypes: acute endometritis and chronic endometritis (CE). Acute endometritis typically occurs after events such as abortion, childbirth, menstruation, uterine curettage, or intrauterine device (IUD) insertion. Clinical manifestations of acute endometritis may include fever, pelvic pain, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Histological examination reveals a significant presence of neutrophils within the endometrial stroma in cases of acute endometritis. Chronic endometritis, on the other hand, is often asymptomatic or presents with nonspecific symptoms. It is a potential cause of infertility. Histopathologically, chronic endometritis is characterized by the presence of plasma cells in the endometrial stroma. Endometritis is predominantly caused by infections and is treated with antibiotics. It frequently arises due to the rupture of membranes during childbirth and is the most common postpartum infection. Puerperal endometritis is significantly more prevalent in patients who have undergone cesarean sections, with an incidence rate 25 times higher than in vaginal deliveries. Most postpartum endometritis cases are polymicrobial, involving both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Causes of Endometritis: Postpartum endometritis results from bacterial ascent from the lower genital tract into the cervix during labor. The vaginal microflora implicated in this process include: Aerobic and anaerobic bacteria such as Alpha-hemolytic streptococci, Corynebacterium, Diphtheroids, Escherichia coli, Enterobacter species (e.g., Enterobacter agglomerans, Enterobacter cloacae, Enterobacter aerogenes), Fusobacterium necrophorum, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Lactobacillus species (e.g., L. crispatus, L. casei, L. jensenii), Mycoplasma genitalium, Mycoplasma hominis, Nondescript streptococci, Prevotella species (e.g., P. bivia, P. melaninogenicus), Staphylococcus epidermidis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum. Chronic endometritis is also caused by infections with various microorganisms, including: Bacteria: Escherichia coli, Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus species, Enterococcus faecalis, Proteus species, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Gardnerella vaginalis, Corynebacterium. Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma species: Mycoplasma genitalium, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum. Yeasts: Candida species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Acute endometritis may also be caused by sexually transmitted pathogens such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Risk Factors: For puerperal endometritis, risk factors include: Cesarean delivery Surgical or instrumental delivery Chorioamnionitis Prolonged rupture of membranes Retained placental fragments Postpartum hemorrhage Frequent vaginal examinations Colonization with Group B Streptococcus (GBS) For chronic endometritis, risk factors include: Prolonged use of intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUDs) Prolonged menstruation Atypical uterine bleeding Fallopian tube obstruction Multiparity History of abortion Bacterial vaginosis Endometrial hyperplasia Submucosal fibroids Endometriosis Endometrial osseous metaplasia Tuberculosis Diagnosis: The diagnosis of endometritis involves clinical evaluation and may include laboratory tests, imaging, and histopathological examination. Specific diagnostic algorithms are used to guide the process. Treatment: Treatment strategies for endometritis depend on the severity of the condition. Mild cases are managed with antibiotics, while moderate to severe cases may require more aggressive interventions, including intravenous antibiotics. Complications such as sepsis, abscess formation, hematoma, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, and necrotizing fasciitis can occur. In severe cases, uterine necrosis may necessitate a hysterectomy to resolve the infection. Surgical drainage may also be required if fluid collections are present. To reduce the risk of endometritis caused by sexually transmitted diseases (STDs): Patients should practice safe sex, including consistent condom use. Routine screening and early diagnosis of STDs in both the patient and their partner are essential. Patients must complete the full course of prescribed treatment for any diagnosed STD. To minimize the risk of endometritis associated with cesarean sections: Prophylactic antibiotics should be administered prior to cesarean deliveries. Routine antepartum screening and treatment of GBS and other infections. Strict hand hygiene practices. Adherence to aseptic techniques during procedures. Minimizing the number of vaginal examinations. Limiting the use of invasive procedures. Avoiding unnecessary episiotomies. Using synthetic sutures. Reducing cesarean delivery rates. Prompt repair of lacerations. Employing standard suture techniques. Administering prophylactic antibiotics for anal sphincter injuries. Important Considerations: Patients should not hesitate to contact their healthcare provider if they notice any signs of infection.
